analysis.one_liner: Lets hospital 'observation' stays count toward Medicare's nursing home coverage rule.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to fix Medicare's observation-stay trap was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on April 14, 2011 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare only pays for nursing home care after a hospital stay if the patient was officially an 'inpatient' for three days. Many seniors, however, spend days in the hospital under cheaper 'observation' status without ever being told they were not admitted, then get stuck with the full nursing home bill. This bill would count those observation days toward the three-day requirement, retroactive to January 1, 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who receive hospital observation services and need skilled nursing care afterward. Under current rules they can be denied nursing home coverage and owe thousands of dollars out of pocket, sometimes after they have already been discharged and billed. The bill also covers back to January 1, 2011 and lets people who were wrongly denied appeal within 90 days of enactment.

how_it_helps.text: Counts outpatient observation days as inpatient days for Medicare's three-day hospital requirement for skilled nursing facility coverage [S2][S3].
Applies to observation stays beginning on or after January 1, 2011, and lets people whose nursing care was already denied appeal within 90 days of enactment [S3].
Deems the end of observation services the hospital discharge date unless the patient is admitted as an inpatient at that point, so the coverage clock runs from the actual stay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program would pay skilled nursing facility bills that previously fell entirely on patients, increasing federal spending. Hospitals' billing practices are not changed by the bill, but federal costs rise.

drawbacks.text: Federal cost: Medicare would take on nursing home bills that patients currently pay themselves, raising program spending at a time when Congress was focused on deficit reduction [S2][S3].

Good-faith objection: the general rule that only inpatient stays count toward the three-day requirement is intended to distinguish brief diagnostic visits from real hospital admissions, and counting observation stays could pull routine stays into a coverage category Congress did not design for them.
The bill addresses only the eligibility clock; it does not change how hospitals bill observation stays, so patients' higher hospital cost-sharing under observation status would remain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: it stops seniors from owing thousands in nursing home bills after hospital stays they believed were admissions. The cost is real but modest relative to Medicare's overall budget, and the bill includes an orderly appeals process for past denials. The main critique is that it papers over the broader observation-status billing problem rather than fixing it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with a bipartisan pair of sponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and never received any further action before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 14, 2011 by Senator John Kerry (D-MA) with Senator Olympia Snowe (R-ME) as co-lead sponsor [S1][S3].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill: 2 Republicans and 5 Democrats [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on April 14, 2011; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The Senate's action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Medicare program's budget and the status quo, in which hospitals keep classifying stays as observation and patients keep paying their own nursing home bills, were preserved. Seniors facing observation stays remained exposed to the full cost of skilled nursing care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Medicare program's budget and status quo

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured a bipartisan co-lead sponsor

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 14, 2011 and never took it up; no markup, vote, or report was scheduled in the 21 months before the Congress ended

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred and never scheduled action on it

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which it could not reach without a committee report or a floor agreement

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: Senator Kerry introduced it with Republican Senator Olympia Snowe as co-lead, and the seven cosponsors included 2 Republicans and 5 Democrats [S4].

industries.note: The bill would make more hospital observation patients eligible for Medicare-covered nursing home care, turning currently denied, self-pay admissions into covered ones. Nursing homes' revenue rises when patients are not stuck with unpayable bills.
The bill does not change how hospitals bill observation stays, so hospital revenue is largely untouched, but it removes a source of patient complaints and billing disputes over observation status.
Medicare would pay nursing home bills that beneficiaries currently bear, raising federal outlays. This is the cost side of a shift of expense from patients to the program.
